back: Check the cache. On a miss, read the database, store the result with a TTL, return it. The application does the work.
Update the database, then delete the cache key so the next read reloads it.
The cache is optional: if it's down, reads fall back to the database and stay correct, just slower.
Pre-loading hot keys into a cache before it takes traffic, to avoid a wave of cold misses hitting the database.
The app reads only from the cache; on a miss the cache's own loader fetches from the database, stores and returns the value.
Concurrent misses for the same key wait on a single load, so one database query serves them all.
Each write updates cache and database synchronously; the client is acknowledged only when both succeed.
Every write pays two hops, and every written value is cached even if never read (pair it with a TTL).
Acknowledge the write once the cache has it; flush to the database asynchronously, often batched.
Acknowledged but unflushed writes are lost if the cache node dies, and the database lags the cache.
View counts, likes, metrics: high-rate updates where batching helps and losing a few seconds is acceptable.
Writes go only to the database (invalidating the key if cached); the cache fills later only if the data is read.
Write-heavy data that's rarely read back (logs, audit events, bulk imports): it avoids filling the cache with entries nobody reads.
Cache-aside reads with update-database-then-delete-key writes, plus a TTL on every key.

front: Why set a TTL whatever the strategy?
back: It bounds how long any bug, missed invalidation or race can serve stale data.
